title: A predictive theory of microbial communities

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a theory that predicts which microbes will coexist, their abundances and what their community will do, using measurable properties of the organisms and their environment. Its central ambition is to make useful predictions without experimentally testing every possible combination of species and conditions. Predicting community composition and predicting community function are distinct goals: knowing which organisms are present does not by itself establish their collective activity.

A concrete starting point is understanding how interactions measured in small groups translate into larger communities. Ishizawa and colleagues demonstrated that measurements from pairs alone missed collective effects in a controlled microbial community, while incorporating three-member combinations improved predictions of community structure. A broader theory would need to establish when such small-group measurements are sufficient, which additional measurements are necessary and how far predictions transfer beyond the conditions used to build the model.

significance.text: If experimentally validated across a clearly defined range of ecosystems, this capability would move microbial ecology toward prospective prediction: forecasting community assembly and responses to perturbations before observing their outcomes. The supplied study provides a limited technical foundation by quantitatively linking interactions to community structure. Extending that connection across environments and to ecological functions would be the larger advance; the field-wide impact remains a conditional assessment.

Potential applications include anticipating changes in agricultural microbiomes, wastewater treatment communities and host-associated microbiomes, all application areas identified in the study. Reliable forecasts could help select interventions and reduce empirical screening. Durable interventions would nevertheless require additional capabilities: delivering the intended change, maintaining it under real conditions and validating the desired outcome. Predicting a community's response does not automatically confer practical control over it.

As an impact assessment, the revolutionary feature would be reliable prediction with manageable measurement requirements, rather than a single formula guaranteed to describe every ecosystem. A theory could be broadly useful while retaining explicit boundaries for particular organisms, environments, timescales and functions. Success in predicting equilibrium composition would also leave open whether the same framework predicts transient dynamics, recovery after disturbance or functional performance.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability in this record is a demonstrated, transferable connection from measurable organism and environmental properties to both community composition and function. The supplied evidence establishes a narrower obstacle: pairwise interaction measurements can fail to explain assembly because interactions expressed in a larger community differ from those inferred from pairs. Learning from trios helped in the studied system, but this does not establish that three-member measurements capture every consequential collective effect.

A practical theory must resolve what to measure and how much experimental information is enough. It must identify conditions under which small-group observations support larger-community predictions without recreating the combinatorial burden the theory is meant to avoid. Substantial residual prediction errors in the supplied study show that improved assembly prediction still leaves room for model development and experimental investigation.

Generalization must explicitly test resource conditions, spatial organization, community membership, host context and assembly history. The paper discusses resource competition and identifies temporal factors such as priority effects, together with stochasticity, as omitted from its analyses; it calls for testing across temporal, spatial and taxonomic contexts. These are concrete research boundaries. The supplied study does not establish the magnitude or mechanism of every proposed dependency across natural ecosystems, nor does its composition result establish a general method for predicting function.

current_state.text: In a PNAS paper published on 5 February 2024, Hidehiro Ishizawa and colleagues studied a controlled community of seven duckweed-associated bacterial strains. Incorporating observations from three-member combinations improved predictions of equilibrium abundance and community structure compared with predictions based on pairwise information. This is a demonstrated advance within one experimental system, with a specific prediction target and controlled conditions.

The main-text results, as documented in the supplied review, report trio-based abundance errors of 22.7–61.2%, compared with 53.5–185.2% for pairwise-based predictions. These reported ranges support improvement while also showing substantial remaining error. They should not be interpreted as general accuracy guarantees, converted into a universal percentage of correct predictions or assumed to describe performance in natural ecosystems.

The study does not establish general prediction of ecological function, transfer across natural environments or prediction of temporal responses. Its discussion identifies host, temporal and taxonomic limitations. The supplied review used a complete, untruncated XML extraction of the main article, including methods and references, with no reported extraction issues. Figure images and supplementary files were unavailable for inspection, limiting independent assessment of those materials while leaving the explicit main-text comparison available as evidence.

Evidence coverage limitation: the supplied search record is empty, so subsequent progress through the review's stated cutoff of 1 November 2026 remains unresolved. The supported 2024 result therefore provides a dated example of progress, rather than a comprehensive account of the field at that cutoff. The missing freshness evidence neither invalidates that result nor establishes that the broader capability remains unachieved today.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: conduct blind, quantitative evaluations on independently selected natural communities and perturbations, covering both composition and explicitly defined functions. Predictions should be recorded before outcomes are measured, include interventions excluded from training and report calibrated uncertainty. These are proposed evaluation criteria, not established field standards or achievements documented by the supplied study.
completion_criteria.label: Blind predictions of community composition and function with calibrated uncertainty

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evaluation design: specify the target organisms, environments, spatial scales and timescales; distinguish equilibrium predictions from temporal forecasts; and define functional endpoints and numerical accuracy thresholds before testing. Compare performance with appropriate simpler baselines, including pairwise models where relevant. Report the observations, sampling effort and computational resources required, so that predictive gains can be judged against their practical cost.
completion_criteria.label: Prediction evaluations report prespecified thresholds, baseline comparisons and resource costs

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirement: independent groups should reproduce performance using disclosed measurement and modeling procedures, including tests of environmental transfer and assembly-history effects. Report failures and conditions outside the validated range. Finite experiments would establish demonstrated breadth within those boundaries, not literal universality. Claims about durable interventions would require additional demonstrations of delivery, persistence and functional benefit.
completion_criteria.label: Independent groups reproduce performance across environments and assembly histories

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: MIC-09, “Forecasting horizontal gene transfer and resistance spread in microbial communities,” shares the challenge of predicting processes within communities, but focuses on mobile genes and resistance rather than overall assembly and function. MIC-10, “Programmable microbial consortia for durable ecosystem functions,” concerns designing and maintaining functional communities. Predictive ecology could inform that design, while successful engineering within a restricted setting would not require solving all of MIC-02.

Roster-based synthesis: MIC-06, “A predictive whole-cell model for microbial design,” addresses prediction within an individual cell; MIC-02 addresses outcomes among interacting populations. Whole-cell models could supply useful organism-level properties without resolving community behavior. MIC-03, “Routine experimental access to microbial dark matter,” could expand the organisms available for measurement and testing, but experimental access and predictive theory remain separate capabilities. MIC-01, “An autonomously reproducing cell built from defined components,” likewise concerns constructing a cell rather than forecasting a community.

Roster-based synthesis: MIC-04, “Reliable nitrogen-fixing microbial partnerships for major cereal crops,” and MIC-07, “Programmable, reversible living therapies in the human microbiome,” are potential application areas for community prediction, with additional requirements for function, persistence and control. MIC-05, “A general platform for targeted, adaptable phage treatment,” and MIC-08, “Broadly effective control of bacterial antibiotic persistence,” concern particular interventions and survival phenomena whose outcomes may depend on community context; neither is equivalent to a general predictive theory.

Roster-based synthesis: MIC-11, “Quantifying how environmental viruses control biogeochemical fluxes,” overlaps with predicting ecosystem functions and interactions involving viruses, while retaining a specific causal and biogeochemical focus. MIC-12, “A causal map from microbial metabolites to host phenotypes,” concerns the connection between microbial products and host outcomes. Community predictions could inform both efforts, but predicting community composition alone would not establish viral control of fluxes or metabolite-mediated causation in hosts.

Transfer to natural ecosystems, functional prediction, transient dynamics and robustness across resource, spatial, host, taxonomic and assembly-history conditions remain unestablished by the supplied study.
The error ranges are preserved as reported in the review; their precise metric definition and aggregation should be clarified before using them as comparative benchmarks.

brief.title: Forecasting how communities of microbes behave
possible: Farmers, wastewater operators and healthcare researchers could forecast how communities of microbes respond to changes before trying them. Measurements of the organisms and their surroundings would predict which microbes coexist, how abundant they become and what they collectively do, without testing every possible combination.
why: Reliable forecasts would help people choose changes to microbial communities with less trial and error. They would connect measurable properties of individual organisms to outcomes that matter in agriculture, wastewater treatment and health.

sources.showed: In a controlled community on duckweed, measurements from trios improved predictions of bacterial abundance over measurements from pairs. The predictions still had substantial errors.
sources.quote: These patterns could be learned from trio combinations, highlighting the importance of observing simple beyond-pairwise combinations to capture actual interspecies relationships.
sources.cited_for: Interactions observed in small groups can improve predictions of larger communities.
sources.not_established: The study did not establish predictions of collective activity or transfer to other environments.

sources.showed: In a preprint, they predicted laboratory community membership from communities grown on foods that microbes process similarly. Growth and released by-products also resembled each other across those foods.
sources.quote: We found that growth rates and secretion profiles were positively correlated across environments when the supplied substrate was metabolically similar.
sources.cited_for: Similar food environments can provide a basis for predicting community membership.
sources.not_established: This did not establish general forecasts of community activity or performance in natural environments.

sources.who: A. Pascual-García, D. W. Rivett, Matt Lloyd Jones and T. Bell
sources.showed: Naturally occurring bacterial communities developed reproducibly when revived in a standard laboratory environment. Small differences in starting membership could nevertheless produce different membership and activity.
sources.quote:
Replicate communities follow reproducible trajectories and the
community dynamics closely map to ecosystem functioning.
sources.cited_for: Community development can be repeatable while remaining sensitive to starting membership.
sources.not_established: Repeatability in a shared laboratory environment does not establish forecasts across changing natural conditions.

sources.showed: A model of how microbes share food explained the balance between groups with different ways of using it. Laboratory communities could also settle into different stable outcomes.
sources.quote: Here, we show that the previously observed family-level convergence in these habitats reflects a reproducible metabolic organization, where the ratio of the dominant metabolic groups can be explained from a simple resource-partitioning model.
sources.cited_for: Food use can explain predictable group-level patterns despite differences in individual species.
sources.not_established: The results do not establish a general theory predicting both membership and activity across ecosystems.

shown: Ishizawa and colleagues improved abundance predictions in a controlled community of seven bacterial strains on duckweed by learning from trios. This shows that relationships measured in pairs can miss effects that emerge in larger groups.

Pascual-García and colleagues found repeatable development and links between membership and activity in naturally occurring communities grown in the laboratory. They also found that small starting differences could send communities toward different outcomes.
missing: Predictions of both membership and collective activity must work in natural communities facing previously untested changes.
Researchers must establish which measurements are sufficient without testing an impractical number of combinations.
Forecasts must transfer across environments, hosts and histories of how communities formed.

milestones.label: Blind forecasts predict membership and activity with reliable uncertainty
milestones.explanation: Forecasts made before results are known would have to predict membership and defined activities in independently chosen natural communities under unfamiliar changes. Their uncertainty estimates would establish when to trust them.

milestones.label: Forecasts meet declared standards at a measured cost
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to define scope, timing and accuracy targets in advance, compare simpler models and report measurement and computing costs. This would establish whether better forecasts justify their practical demands.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce forecasts across environments and community histories
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce performance across environments and histories of community formation using disclosed procedures, reporting failures and limits. This would establish the breadth of reliable prediction.

uncertain: It remains unclear when measurements from small groups capture enough of the interactions in larger communities.
The required accuracy, activities to predict and acceptable measurement costs still need to be defined.
Predicting a settled community may require different tools from predicting its development or recovery after disturbance.

page.title: Predictive theory of microbial community structure and function
page.definition: A mechanistic framework predicts which microbes coexist, their abundances and their collective activities from organism traits and environmental conditions. Its predictions transfer beyond the communities and conditions used to develop it without testing every possible species combination.

goal.need: On 5 February 2024, Ishizawa et al. reported measurements of all 127 nonempty combinations of seven duckweed-associated bacterial strains. Learning from trios reduced reported abundance prediction errors from 53.5–185.2% to 22.7–61.2%. Predicting untested combinations would reduce this experimental burden; these composition results do not establish prediction of community function.

figures.caption: Abundance prediction errors in the seven-strain duckweed system
figures.note: Ranges span seven strains. The 127 combinations had 5–12 independent flasks each. RMSPE is the study’s abundance-error metric; lower values indicate less error.

completion.title: Independent experiments validate joint predictions of microbial composition and function across environments.
completion.criterion: Within a declared domain of microbial habitats, one mechanistic framework predicts taxon persistence, abundances and a measured community process rate after environmental changes excluded from model development, without assaying every community combination. Predictions meet endpoint-specific acceptance limits fixed before outcomes are known. An independent team reproduces the result in independently sampled environments within that domain. This provisional Atlas test has no field-agreed numerical accuracy, sample-size or measurement-cost threshold.
completion.set_by: Atlas; provisional operational criterion because no external joint completion test was identified.
completion.basis: Searches of NRC recommendations, NSF 20-513, DOE’s 2010 Knowledgebase and April 2026 reports, mSystems workshop recommendations and prediction challenges found no accepted joint completion test or numerical acceptance limits. NSF requests “generalizable principles”; DOE requests prediction “across time and space”. This provisional test operationalizes those goals within a declared domain.

milestones.title: A model explains metabolic roles and interactions in a microbial community.
milestones.criterion: Construct a descriptive model of community members’ metabolic roles and interactions, DOE’s first stage; no numerical pass threshold is specified. In the study issued on 19 January 2022, Estrela et al. parameterized a resource-partitioning model using 47 Enterobacteriaceae and 18 Pseudomonas isolates. Across 846 isolate pairs, the predicted median respirator/fermenter ratio was 0.31, compared with an observed 16S-rRNA sequence-abundance ratio of 0.29 in 92 glucose-grown communities.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Department of Energy, Knowledgebase System Development Workshop report, section 4b.1, first stage: Understanding.
milestones.threshold_quote: metabolic role of the members within the community and their interactions.

milestones.title: A model predicts microbial metabolic processes and responses to environmental conditions.
milestones.criterion: Simulate community metabolic processes and predict responses of activity or composition to environmental conditions, DOE’s second stage; no accuracy cutoff is specified. Vila et al.’s 28 October 2023 preprint, not peer reviewed, examined 343 communities from 23 inocula across 48 carbon sources. Across inocula, composition predictions improved over a random-environment null at family and clade levels, but not at exact-sequence-variant level. On 14 October 2025, Andersen et al. reported abundance forecasts from 4,709 samples in 24 wastewater plants, training each plant’s model separately. These studies do not establish joint transferable prediction.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Department of Energy, Knowledgebase System Development Workshop report, section 4b.1, second stage: Prediction.
milestones.threshold_quote: the response of community activity or composition to environmental conditions.

milestones.title: A model passes prospective composition-and-function tests in a new microbial habitat.
milestones.criterion: In a habitat excluded from model development, one framework meets predeclared prediction limits for taxon abundances and a measured community process rate after an environmental perturbation. No external joint endpoint or error cutoff was found. Pascual-García et al., published on 31 March 2025, revived 275 rain-pool communities in four laboratory replicates each: 1,100 microcosms grown for 7 days at 22 °C. Composition trajectories were reproducible and associated with functional differences; the experiment did not validate prospective predictions under an untested field perturbation.
milestones.set_by: Atlas; provisional interpretation of NSF’s generalization goal and DOE’s environmental prediction goal, preceding independent replication.

not_found: No externally defined acceptance test for a transferable theory jointly predicting microbial composition and measured community function was identified.
No common numerical limits for prediction error, validation breadth or measurement burden were found in the examined agency and committee documents.
No independent prospective replication satisfying the provisional joint completion criterion was identified.

results.finding: A model quantified 1,344 interaction coefficients among seven duckweed-associated bacterial strains.
results.detail: The model describes context-dependent interactions, but does not identify the strains’ individual metabolic roles or mechanisms.
results.quote: Assigning the abundance data to this equation yielded a total of 1,344 interaction coefficients (  C ij  ), each of which characterizes the actual interaction forces of species  j  on  i  under specific community context (corresponding to an edge in  Fig. 2 ).

results.finding: Trio-based predictions of seven strains’ abundances in 64 larger communities had errors of 22.7–61.2%.
results.detail: The model predicts composition from smaller combinations, but does not simulate metabolic processes or test responses to changing environmental conditions.
results.quote: As the results, the predicted abundances of the seven SBC members showed a linear relationship with the observed values, with relative mean square percentage errors (RMSPE) of 22.7 to 61.2% ( Fig. 5 C ), which is substantially better than those from the pairwise-based predictions (RMSPE of 53.5 to 185.2%)

results.finding: Across 343 communities, composition predictions beat a random-environment null at family and clade levels when using different inocula.
results.detail: The comparative approach used modeled metabolic similarity and observed community compositions. It did not simulate community metabolic processes; cross-inoculum predictions did not improve on the null at exact-sequence-variant level.
results.quote: When using a different inoculum the comparative approach performed quantitatively similarly to the null at the ESV level, marginally better at the Genus Level and substantively better at the Family and Clade level

results.finding: A composition model tested on 275 communities predicted outcomes for three held-out replicates.
results.detail: A transformation fitted using one replicate predicted the others in the same standardized environment. The study did not simulate metabolic processes or test responses across environmental conditions.
results.quote:

results.finding: Across 1,100 microcosms, two final community classes differed in measured degradation and activity.
results.detail: The study linked reproducible composition trajectories to function, but did not prospectively validate joint abundance and process-rate predictions against predeclared limits in a new habitat after a perturbation.
results.quote:
Final Class 1 communities had higher degradation rates
and enzymatic activity, while Final Class 2 communities had a higher
per-cell investment but lower cell numbers, implying that they were
growing inefﬁciently (Fig.5b).

results.finding: A resource-partitioning model predicted a median respirator-to-fermenter ratio of 0.31 across 846 isolate pairs.
results.detail: The model describes glucose use by fermenters and cross-feeding of acetate to respirators. The observed median ratio was 0.29 in 92 glucose-grown communities.
results.quote: By empirically parameterizing the model with our collection of F and R isolates, we find a median predicted R/F ratio of 0.31 (Q1 = 0.22, Q3 = 0.43, N = 846), very close to the experimentally observed median R/F ratio of 0.29 (Q1 = 0.17, Q3 = 0.69, N = 92) in our communities

results.finding: A metabolic model predicted a higher respirator-to-fermenter ratio for non-fermentable substrates; communities were assembled on 5 alternative carbon sources.
results.detail: The observed ratio was similar across the sugars tested and increased on citrate and glutamine, consistent with the model's qualitative prediction.
results.quote: This finding is consistent with our model, which predicts that because respirators have a growth advantage on non-fermentable carbon sources relative to fermenters, respirators are favored and fermenters disfavored; therefore, the R/F ratio should increase.

results.finding: A consumer-resource model predicted composition across 960 algal communities with 83.4% mean accuracy.
results.detail: The model simulated resource consumption and abundance across nutrient conditions, including conditions not used to fit monocultures. Accuracy was measured by Bray–Curtis similarity.
results.quote: it was well-predicted by the mechanistic model, with a mean accuracy of 83.4%

results.finding: A model predicted nitrate utilization dynamics across soils and pH perturbations; measurements covered more than 1,500 soil microcosms.
results.detail: The model described community-level nitrate metabolism. Its parameters were fitted to measured nitrate dynamics across conditions; the text does not establish transferable predictions for unseen soils or conditions.

results.finding: A consumer-resource model described resource use and competition among 12 phytoplankton species.
results.detail: The model used monoculture growth data to estimate resource requirements and consumption, representing interactions through competition for shared resources.
results.quote: Here, we integrate a mechanistic consumer-resource model with the growth of 12 phytoplankton species in monoculture over a range of nitrate, ammonium or phosphorous concentrations.

results.finding: The model predicted composition across 960 phytoplankton communities under varied resource conditions.
results.detail: The tests included resource conditions absent from monoculture parameterization, but did not establish joint predictions of composition and a measured community process rate in a new habitat against predeclared limits.
results.quote: We find that the mechanistic approach accurately predicts the composition of 960 communities across species richness and resource conditions.

results.finding: A model fit nitrate utilization dynamics across 20 soils with less than 10% error per data point.
results.detail: The model describes nitrate-utilizing biomass and its resource limitation, but combines taxa into one effective biomass rather than modeling individual members and their interactions.

results.finding: In four additional soils, the model described nitrate dynamics and the same qualitative functional regimes appeared.
results.detail: The additional soils were subjected to pH perturbations, but model parameters were fitted to their data. The paper does not report prospective taxon-abundance and process-rate predictions meeting predeclared limits.

results.finding: DySCoMeMo reconstructed metabolic interactions in synthetic gut communities containing up to 25 taxa.
results.detail: The model inferred metabolite-mediated cross-feeding and species’ metabolic roles from predicted uptake and secretion fluxes.
results.quote: DySCoMeMo enables reconstruction of time-resolved metabolite-mediated microbial trophic interaction networks by identifying directed cross-feeding relationships from predicted secretion and uptake fluxes

results.finding: DySCoMeMo forecast outcomes for 761 synthetic community combinations; high-richness butyrate predictions had Pearson’s r = 0.81.
results.detail: The held-out synthetic communities were not a new habitat after an environmental perturbation. The mouse perturbation analysis used abundance trajectories from that dataset to infer model parameters; no predeclared joint abundance and process-rate limits are reported.
results.quote: These predictions were evaluated against experimentally measured metabolite levels, enabling a direct assessment of DySCoMeMo’s ability to forecast metabolic outcome under previously unseen conditions

results.finding: A salinity-response model predicted shifts toward faster growers; all 8 tested bacterial pairs showed increased advantage for faster growers.
results.detail: The model simulated community growth and composition under salinity stress, but did not simulate specific metabolic processes.
results.quote:
We found that, in all eight competitions tested, the faster-growing

results.finding: A resource-competition model accounted for most pairwise interactions among 15 human gut commensals.
results.detail: The model system was grown in vitro in complex media; cross-feeding and pH-mediated interactions improved coexistence predictions.
results.quote: We applied our framework to an in vitro model system comprising 15 human gut commensals in complex media and showed that a simple model of resource competition accounted for most pairwise interactions.
